symmetry-charge-identity-386855df.interpretation: In this relation, $\delta S$ represents the first variation of the action functional $S = \int L \, dt$ under an infinitesimal global continuous symmetry transformation $\delta q^i$. The condition $\delta S = 0$ denotes invariance of the action functional under this transformation. The bidirectional connective $\iff$ denotes logical and physical equivalence on-shell (when the Euler-Lagrange equations of motion are satisfied). The variable $Q$ denotes the Noether charge generated by the continuous symmetry, defined canonically by $Q = \sum_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}^i} \delta q^i - \Lambda$ for quasi-invariant Lagrangians, and $\dot{Q} = \frac{dQ}{dt}$ is its total time derivative. Thus, $\dot{Q} = 0$ signifies strict conservation of the charge over time.
symmetry-charge-identity-386855df.symmetry_origin: Rooted in Noether's First Theorem relating continuous global spacetime and internal Lie group symmetries (such as $U(1)$ gauge transformations, spatial translations, and temporal translations) to dynamical conservation laws.
symmetry-charge-identity-386855df.limits_and_boundary: Holds strictly on-shell for continuous, differentiable transformations in systems without non-conservative friction or quantum anomalies. In quantum field theory, anomalous symmetry breaking leads to $\langle \partial_\mu j^\mu \rangle \neq 0$, violating the classical identity.
symmetry-charge-identity-386855df.conceptual_definition: The Symmetry-Charge Identity encapsulates Noether's First Theorem in global variational calculus: a continuous Lie group transformation leaves the action invariant ($\delta S = 0$) up to boundary terms if and only if the corresponding generalized Noether charge $Q$ is constant along physical trajectories ($\dot{Q} = \frac{dQ}{dt} = 0$).
symmetry-charge-identity-386855df.intuitive_summary: Every continuous symmetry of the laws of physics generates a corresponding conserved quantity, and conversely, every conserved charge generates a continuous symmetry of the dynamics.
symmetry-charge-identity-386855df.description: Expresses the fundamental equivalence between the continuous off-shell invariance of an action functional and the on-shell temporal conservation of the associated Noether charge.

non-local-interaction-5aae4fab.title: Abraham-Lorentz Radiation Reaction Force (SI Formulation)

non-local-interaction-5aae4fab.interpretation: The term $\mathbf{F}_{\text{react}}$ represents the radiation reaction force vector in newtons ($\text{N}$). The constant prefactor contains the elementary electric charge $e$, the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c$. The vector $\dot{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{a}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}}{\mathrm{d}t^3}$ denotes the time derivative of the acceleration vector (kinematic jerk).
non-local-interaction-5aae4fab.symmetry_origin: Originates from global spacetime translation invariance and local $U(1)$ electromagnetic gauge invariance via the coupled Maxwell-Lorentz equations, reflecting the self-consistent conservation of total four-momentum.
non-local-interaction-5aae4fab.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of uniform acceleration ($\dot{\mathbf{a}} \to 0$), the Abraham-Lorentz self-force vanishes identically. In the relativistic domain ($v \to c$), the expression generalizes to the relativistic Abraham-Lorentz-Dirac four-force. At microscopic scales, classical point-charge self-interaction leads to run-away solutions or pre-acceleration unless regularized by quantum electrodynamics (QED).
non-local-interaction-5aae4fab.conceptual_definition: The Abraham-Lorentz force $\mathbf{F}_{\text{react}} = \frac{e^2}{6\pi \varepsilon_0 c^3} \dot{\mathbf{a}}$ quantifies the radiative reaction force (or self-force) exerted by a point particle's own electromagnetic field upon itself. Arising from the conservation of energy and momentum in classical electrodynamics, the force is directly proportional to the time derivative of the acceleration (the kinematic jerk $\dot{\mathbf{a}}$).
non-local-interaction-5aae4fab.intuitive_summary: When a charged particle accelerates, it radiates electromagnetic waves that carry energy and momentum away from the system. By Newton's third law and energy conservation, this radiated field pushes back on the particle itself, producing a recoil force proportional to the jerk.
non-local-interaction-5aae4fab.description: Calculates the non-relativistic electromagnetic self-force acting on an accelerating charged particle due to its own emission of dipole radiation.

electron-heat-e87b2637.title: Characteristic Time for Thermal Diffusion

\\tau_{\\mathrm{diff}}.name: Characteristic Diffusion Time
\\tau_{\\mathrm{diff}}.description: The approximate timescale for heat to diffuse over a characteristic length scale.

R.name: Characteristic Length Scale
R.description: The typical distance over which the diffusion process occurs.

c.name: Volumetric Heat Capacity
c.description: The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of a unit volume of a substance by one degree Kelvin. It is the product of density ($\rho$) and specific heat capacity ($c_p$).

\\lambda.name: Thermal Conductivity
\\lambda.description: A measure of a material's intrinsic ability to conduct heat.

electron-heat-e87b2637.interpretation: The formula $\tau_{\mathrm{diff}} \approx \frac{R^2 c}{\lambda}$ provides the characteristic timescale for thermal diffusion, often derived from dimensional analysis of the heat equation $\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha \nabla^2 T$. The time $\tau_{\mathrm{diff}}$ scales with the square of the characteristic length, $R^2$, which is a hallmark of diffusive processes. The numerator contains the volumetric heat capacity $c$ (in units of J·m⁻³·K⁻¹), representing the material's ability to store thermal energy per unit volume. A higher value of $c$ implies more energy is needed to change the temperature, thus increasing the diffusion time. The denominator features the thermal conductivity $\lambda$ (in units of W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹), which measures the material's efficiency in transporting heat. A higher conductivity facilitates faster heat transfer, reducing $\tau_{\mathrm{diff}}$. The ratio $\alpha = \lambda/c$ is defined as the thermal diffusivity (in m²·s⁻¹), allowing the formula to be written more compactly as $\tau_{\mathrm{diff}} \approx R^2/\alpha$.
electron-heat-e87b2637.symmetry_origin: This relation is not derived from a fundamental symmetry in the sense of Noether's theorem. It is a phenomenological scaling law derived from the heat equation, which is a macroscopic manifestation of energy conservation applied to statistical ensembles of particles.
electron-heat-e87b2637.limits_and_boundary: The formula describes a classical, macroscopic process. In the limit of a perfect thermal conductor ($\lambda \to \infty$), the diffusion time $\tau_{\mathrm{diff}} \to 0$. Conversely, for a perfect thermal insulator ($\lambda \to 0$), $\tau_{\mathrm{diff}} \to \infty$. As the characteristic length scale $R \to \infty$, the time required for diffusion also approaches infinity. If the volumetric heat capacity $c \to \infty$, the material acts as an infinite heat sink, and $\tau_{\mathrm{diff}} \to \infty$ as it takes infinite energy to change the local temperature.
electron-heat-e87b2637.conceptual_definition: The characteristic time for thermal diffusion, $\tau_{\mathrm{diff}}$, is the approximate time required for heat to propagate across a characteristic distance $R$ within a medium. It is directly proportional to the square of this distance, $R^2$, and the volumetric heat capacity $c$ of the medium, and inversely proportional to the material's thermal conductivity $\lambda$. This relationship arises from the parabolic nature of the heat equation.
electron-heat-e87b2637.intuitive_summary: Imagine dropping a hot pebble into a cool, still pond. The time it takes for the warmth to spread a certain distance doesn't just double if the distance doubles; it quadruples. This formula captures that idea: spreading heat out takes much longer over larger distances, and materials that are good at holding heat (high heat capacity) or bad at conducting it (low thermal conductivity) will slow the process down even more.
electron-heat-e87b2637.description: This formula provides an estimate for the characteristic timescale over which a thermal gradient dissipates via diffusion across a characteristic length scale in a material.

initial-accuracy-4dd8bea1.title: Density Parameter Evolution in a Radiation-Dominated Universe

\\dot{a}.name: Time derivative of scale factor
\\dot{a}.description: The rate of change of the dimensionless cosmological scale factor with respect to cosmic time.

t.name: Cosmic time
t.description: Proper time measured by a comoving observer since the cosmological singularity.

\\Omega.name: Total density parameter
\\Omega.description: Ratio of total energy density $\rho$ to the critical energy density $\rho_c$.

initial-accuracy-4dd8bea1.interpretation: The relation links the kinematic evolution of the cosmic scale factor $a(t)$ to the dynamical density parameter $\Omega(t) \equiv \rho(t)/\rho_c(t)$. The time derivative $\dot{a} \propto t^{-1/2}$ represents the decelerating expansion velocity driven by a radiation equation of state $p = \rho/3$. The second relation, $|\Omega - 1| \propto t$, shows that the deviation from critical density $\rho_c = 3H^2/(8\pi G)$ grows linearly with cosmic time $t$, illustrating the instability of $\Omega = 1$ without an early epoch of accelerated expansion (cosmic inflation).
initial-accuracy-4dd8bea1.symmetry_origin: Derived from the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric under maximal spatial symmetry (spatial homogeneity and isotropy, $SO(3) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^3$ or $SO(4) / SO(3,1)$), governed by the Einstein field equations with a stress-energy tensor obeying local energy-momentum conservation $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$.
initial-accuracy-4dd8bea1.limits_and_boundary: As cosmic time $t \to 0$, $|\Omega - 1| \to 0$, requiring extreme initial fine-tuning at the Planck scale. As $t \to \infty$ in the radiation regime, $|\Omega - 1| \to \infty$, driving the universe rapidly toward extreme open or closed curvature regimes unless interrupted by matter domination or inflation.
initial-accuracy-4dd8bea1.conceptual_definition: In standard Big Bang cosmology described by the Friedmann equations, the fractional deviation from spatial flatness satisfies $|\Omega(t) - 1| = \frac{|k|}{a^2 H^2} = \frac{|k|}{\dot{a}^2}$. For a radiation-dominated universe with equation of state $w = 1/3$, the scale factor scales as $a(t) \propto t^{1/2}$, yielding an expansion velocity $\dot{a}(t) \propto t^{-1/2}$. Consequently, the deviation from spatial flatness grows linearly with cosmic time, $|\Omega(t) - 1| \propto t$, rendering flat spatial geometry an unstable fixed point under standard decelerating expansion.
initial-accuracy-4dd8bea1.intuitive_summary: In a universe filled with decelerating radiation, the expansion slows down over time. This makes any initial tiny departure from perfect spatial flatness amplify steadily, requiring extreme fine-tuning of the initial density in standard cosmology.
initial-accuracy-4dd8bea1.description: Demonstrates the temporal divergence of the cosmic density parameter from unity in a radiation-dominated Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) universe, underpinning the classical cosmological flatness problem.

point-magnetism-7679979d.title: Point Magnetism

B.name: Magnetic Field
B.description: The magnetic field vector at a point in space, measured in Teslas (T).

\\mu_0.name: Permeability of Free Space
\\mu_0.description: A fundamental physical constant representing the capability of a vacuum to permit magnetic field lines, approximately 4\pi \times 10^{-7} N/A^2.

q.name: Electric Charge
q.description: The magnitude of the point electric charge, measured in Coulombs (C).

v.name: Velocity of Charge
v.description: The velocity vector of the point charge, measured in meters per second (m/s).

\\hat{r}.name: Unit Vector to Observation Point
\\hat{r}.description: A unit vector pointing from the position of the charge to the point where the magnetic field is being measured. It is dimensionless.

r.name: Distance to Observation Point
r.description: The scalar distance from the point charge to the point where the magnetic field is being measured, in meters (m).

\\pi.name: Pi constant
\\pi.description: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter (approx. 3.14159).

point-magnetism-7679979d.interpretation: The equation ($\mathbf{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \frac{q\mathbf{v} \times \hat{\mathbf{r}$}}{r^2}$) calculates the magnetic field vector ( \mathbf{B} ) . The constant ( \mu_0 ) is the permeability of free space, a fundamental constant that quantifies how magnetic fields permeate a vacuum. The term ($q$) represents the electric charge of the point particle, measured in Coulombs (C). The velocity vector ( \mathbf{v} ) , in meters per second (m/s), indicates the motion of the charge. The vector ( \hat{\mathbf{r}$}$) is a unit vector pointing from the position of the charge to the point where the magnetic field is being measured. The term ($r^2$) signifies the square of the distance from the charge to the point of observation, measured in square meters (m^2). The cross product ( \mathbf{v} \times \hat{\mathbf{r}}$) determines the direction of the magnetic field, which is perpendicular to both the velocity of the charge and the line connecting the charge to the observation point, following the right-hand rule. The overall magnitude of the magnetic field decreases with the square of the distance and is directly proportional to the charge and its speed.
point-magnetism-7679979d.symmetry_origin: This formula is a direct consequence of the relativistic nature of electromagnetism and can be derived from Maxwell's equations. It is a specific case of the Biot-Savart law for a single moving point charge, which itself can be derived from the fundamental principles of electromagnetism, such as Gauss's law for magnetism and Ampere's law, or from the Liénard-Wiechert potentials for a charged particle.
point-magnetism-7679979d.limits_and_boundary: As the velocity ($\mathbf{v}$) approaches zero, the magnetic field ($\mathbf{B}$) approaches zero, indicating that a stationary charge produces no magnetic field. As the distance ( $r$) approaches infinity, the magnetic field ($\mathbf{B}$) approaches zero, as expected for any field that falls off with distance. If the velocity vector ($\mathbf{v}$) is parallel or antiparallel to the unit vector ($\hat{\mathbf{r}}$), the cross product is zero, and thus the magnetic field ($\mathbf{B}$) is zero at that point.
point-magnetism-7679979d.conceptual_definition: The formula describes the magnetic field ($\mathbf{B}$) produced by a point charge ( $q$) moving with a velocity ($\mathbf{v}$) at a specific point in space. It is a fundamental equation in electromagnetism, often referred to as the Biot-Savart law for a moving point charge, and quantifies the magnetic field generated by this elementary current element.
point-magnetism-7679979d.intuitive_summary: A moving charge generates a magnetic field that is proportional to the charge's velocity and inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the charge, with its direction determined by the cross product of the velocity and the position vector.

natural-path-adcbea6f.title: Levi-Civita Connection Components (Christoffel Symbols of the Second Kind)

\\Gamma^k_{ij}.name: Christoffel symbol of the second kind
\\Gamma^k_{ij}.description: Components of the symmetric, metric-compatible Levi-Civita connection

g^{kl}.name: Inverse metric tensor

g_{ij}.description: Covariant metric tensor components describing spacetime geometry

\\partial_i.name: Partial derivative operator
\\partial_i.description: Coordinate partial derivative with respect to coordinate x^i

x^i.name: Spacetime coordinate
x^i.description: Coordinate component specifying position in the spacetime manifold

\\tau.name: Affine parameter / Proper time
\\tau.description: Affine trajectory parameter along a timelike or null geodesic path

natural-path-adcbea6f.interpretation: In the explicit formulation $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} g^{kl} \left( \partial_i g_{jl} + \partial_j g_{il} - \partial_l g_{ij} \right)$, the symbols $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ represent the affine connection coefficients. The term $g^{kl}$ is the contravariant (inverse) metric tensor used to raise the index $l$. The partial derivatives $\partial_i g_{jl} = \frac{\partial g_{jl}}{\partial x^i}$ quantify spatial and temporal variations in spacetime geometry. Although $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ is non-tensorial under general coordinate transformations, it dictates the inertial correction in the geodesic equation $\frac{d^2 x^k}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^k_{ij} \frac{dx^i}{d\tau} \frac{dx^j}{d\tau} = 0$, where $\tau$ is an affine parameter.
natural-path-adcbea6f.symmetry_origin: Fundamental Theorem of Riemannian Geometry: on any semi-Riemannian manifold, there exists a unique symmetric (torsion-free, $\text{Diff}(M)$ invariant) connection that preserves the metric tensor (metric compatibility / local Lorentz invariance).
natural-path-adcbea6f.limits_and_boundary: In flat Minkowski spacetime with Cartesian coordinates, $\partial_k g_{ij} = 0$, leading to identically vanishing connection coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij} = 0$. By the Equivalence Principle, for any point $P$ in curved spacetime, Riemann normal coordinates can be chosen such that $\Gamma^k_{ij}(P) = 0$, recovering the local inertial frame.
natural-path-adcbea6f.conceptual_definition: The Christoffel symbols of the second kind, $\Gamma^k_{ij}$, specify the components of the Levi-Civita connection in a coordinate basis. Derived uniquely from the metric compatibility condition $\nabla_k g_{ij} = 0$ and the torsion-free condition $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}$, they quantify the rate of change of coordinate basis vectors across spacetime and govern parallel transport and geodesic trajectory equations.
natural-path-adcbea6f.intuitive_summary: The Christoffel symbols act as the gravitational 'force field' or inertial acceleration coefficients in curved spacetime, encoding the twisting and stretching of coordinate grids through first derivatives of the metric.
natural-path-adcbea6f.description: Expresses the torsion-free, metric-compatible affine connection (Christoffel symbols of the second kind) in terms of first partial derivatives of the metric tensor and the inverse metric.

heisenberg-force-303e45e2.title: Heisenberg Force

P.name: Heisenberg Force/Pressure
P.description: Represents the magnitude of the repulsive quantum mechanical force or pressure arising from the uncertainty principle and the Pauli Exclusion Principle for a system of fermions.

\\hbar.name: Reduced Planck Constant
\\hbar.description: A fundamental physical constant representing the quantum of angular momentum and energy, crucial in quantum mechanics. It is defined as the Planck constant $h$ divided by $2\pi$.

n.name: Number Density
n.description: The number of particles per unit volume in the system. A higher number density implies that particles are more closely packed.

m.name: Particle Mass
m.description: The mass of an individual fermion particle in the system.

heisenberg-force-303e45e2.interpretation: In the given proportionality, $P$ represents a pressure or force that is directly proportional to the square of the reduced Planck constant, $\hbar$. The reduced Planck constant, $\hbar = h / (2\pi)$, is a fundamental constant of nature that quantifies the discrete nature of energy and momentum at the quantum level. The term $n^{5/3}$ indicates that this force is strongly dependent on the number density of particles, $n$, meaning it increases significantly as particles are packed more closely together. The exponent $5/3$ arises from considering the three-dimensional nature of the system and the Fermi-Dirac statistics governing fermions. Finally, the proportionality is inversely related to the mass of the particles, $m$. This means that lighter fermions exert a greater Heisenberg force at a given density than heavier ones.
heisenberg-force-303e45e2.symmetry_origin: The Heisenberg Force is a direct consequence of the Pauli Exclusion Principle, which is a fundamental principle of quantum mechanics stemming from the antisymmetry of the many-body wavefunction for identical fermions. This antisymmetry ensures that no two fermions can occupy the same quantum state, leading to an effective 'repulsion' that contributes to the pressure.
heisenberg-force-303e45e2.limits_and_boundary: As the particle density $n$ approaches zero (dilute system), the Heisenberg Force approaches zero, as expected because there is ample space for particles to avoid occupying the same states. As the particle density $n$ approaches infinity (highly compressed system), the Heisenberg Force increases significantly, becoming a dominant factor in the system's pressure. As the particle mass $m$ approaches infinity, the Heisenberg Force approaches zero, as heavier particles are less affected by quantum confinement effects compared to lighter particles at the same density.
heisenberg-force-303e45e2.conceptual_definition: The Heisenberg Force, represented by the proportionality $P \propto \hbar^2 n^{5/3} / m$, describes a quantum mechanical effect that arises from the uncertainty principle, particularly in systems of interacting fermions. It quantifies a repulsive pressure or force that prevents identical fermions from occupying the same quantum state, thus contributing to the stability of matter and phenomena like the degeneracy pressure in white dwarf stars and neutron stars.
heisenberg-force-303e45e2.intuitive_summary: The Heisenberg Force is a quantum repulsion that arises from the Pauli exclusion principle, becoming stronger with denser fermion systems and lighter particles.

flux-source-9dfd9cd0.title: Poisson's Equation for Gravity (Weak-Field General Relativity)

\\nabla^2.name: Laplace Operator
\\nabla^2.description: The divergence of the gradient of a scalar field, often written as $\nabla \cdot \nabla$.

\\Phi.name: Gravitational Potential
\\Phi.description: The scalar potential associated with the gravitational field, representing potential energy per unit mass.

G.name: Newtonian Gravitational Constant
G.description: The empirical physical constant quantifying the strength of the gravitational force.

\\rho.name: Mass-Energy Density
\\rho.description: The density of mass and energy in a given volume. Corresponds to the $T_{00}$ component of the stress-energy tensor.

P.name: Pressure
P.description: The isotropic pressure within the matter source. Corresponds to the spatial diagonal components of the stress-energy tensor.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: A universal physical constant, the speed of all massless particles and associated fields in vacuum.

flux-source-9dfd9cd0.interpretation:
The equation $
abla^2 \Phi = 4\pi G (ho + 3P/c^2)$ relates the Laplacian of the gravitational potential, $
abla^2 \Phi$, to its sources. The Laplacian $
abla^2 \Phi$ represents the divergence of the gravitational field, quantifying how much the field 'spreads out' from a point. The right-hand side details the sources: $ho$ is the mass-energy density, the familiar source from Newtonian gravity. The term $3P/c^2$, where $P$ is pressure and $c$ is the speed of light, is a purely relativistic correction. It signifies that pressure contributes to the gravitational field, a consequence of the fact that the source of gravity in General Relativity is the stress-energy tensor, not just mass. The factor of 3 arises from the trace of this tensor for a perfect fluid.
flux-source-9dfd9cd0.symmetry_origin: Derived as a weak-field approximation of Einstein's Field Equations, which are founded on the principle of general covariance (diffeomorphism invariance). This fundamental symmetry ensures the laws of physics are independent of the observer's coordinate system and state of motion.
flux-source-9dfd9cd0.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit where the speed of light $c \to \infty$, or for pressureless dust where $P=0$, the equation reduces to the classical Poisson's equation for gravity, $\nabla^2 \Phi = 4\pi G \rho$. In a vacuum where both $\rho=0$ and $P=0$, it becomes Laplace's equation, $\nabla^2 \Phi = 0$. This formula is only valid in the weak-field limit (where $|\Phi|/c^2 \ll 1$) and for static or quasi-static matter distributions.
flux-source-9dfd9cd0.conceptual_definition: This equation is the weak-field and static-source approximation of Einstein's Field Equations. It extends the classical Poisson's equation for gravity, $\nabla^2 \Phi = 4\pi G \rho$, by including pressure $P$ as a source of gravitation. The term $(\rho + 3P/c^2)$ represents the effective gravitational source density, derived from the trace of the stress-energy tensor, highlighting that in General Relativity, all forms of energy and momentum—not just mass—curve spacetime.
flux-source-9dfd9cd0.intuitive_summary: In Einstein's theory, gravity is caused not just by mass, but by all energy and momentum. This equation reveals that pressure, a form of energy, also creates gravity. For extremely dense objects like neutron stars, the immense internal pressure significantly increases their gravitational pull beyond what their mass alone would suggest.
flux-source-9dfd9cd0.description: A generalization of Newton's law of universal gravitation, this equation describes the gravitational potential generated by mass-energy and pressure in the weak-field, static limit of Einstein's General Relativity.

solar-system-check-a5d55a52.title: Logarithmic Gradient of Keplerian Orbital Velocity

v.description: Circular orbital speed of a test particle around the central mass

r.description: Radial distance from the center of mass to the orbiting body

solar-system-check-a5d55a52.interpretation: The term $\mathrm{d} \ln v = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v}$ represents the fractional change in orbital speed, while $\mathrm{d} \ln r = \frac{\mathrm{d}r}{r}$ represents the fractional change in orbital radius. The constant value $-\frac{1}{2}$ is the power-law index arising directly from the balance between Newtonian gravitational acceleration $g(r) = \frac{GM}{r^2}$ and centripetal acceleration $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$. A measured slope steeper or shallower than $-1/2$ signals non-Keplerian dynamics, such as an extended mass distribution $M(r)$ or non-gravitational forces.
solar-system-check-a5d55a52.symmetry_origin: Originates from the scale invariance of the inverse-square gravitational force under Kepler's third law scaling transformation ($r \to \lambda r$, $t \to \lambda^{3/2} t$, $v \to \lambda^{-1/2} v$) in a central field with rotational $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ symmetry.
solar-system-check-a5d55a52.limits_and_boundary: Valid strictly for test particles in circular orbits around a dominant central mass $M$. In the limit $r \to 0$, relativistic corrections mandate the use of the Schwarzschild effective potential where the profile deviates and reaches the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). In the limit $r \to \infty$ within galaxies, the slope transitions from $-1/2$ toward $0$ due to the presence of extended dark matter halos.
solar-system-check-a5d55a52.conceptual_definition: The logarithmic derivative $\frac{\mathrm{d} \ln v}{\mathrm{d} \ln r} = -\frac{1}{2}$ characterizes the local power-law exponent of the orbital velocity profile $v(r)$ for test particles on circular orbits in a central gravitational field governed by a point mass or external spherical mass distribution. Integrating this relation recovers the standard Keplerian decline $v(r) \propto r^{-1/2}$, distinguishing point-mass systems from flat rotation curves ($\mathrm{d} \ln v / \mathrm{d} \ln r = 0$) characteristic of galactic dark matter halos.
solar-system-check-a5d55a52.intuitive_summary: If you double the distance from the central star, the orbital speed drops by a factor of $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$, which corresponds to a constant logarithmic slope of $-0.5$ on a log-log rotation curve.
solar-system-check-a5d55a52.description: Expresses the scale-invariant power-law slope of circular orbital velocity with respect to radial distance under a point-mass Newtonian gravitational potential.

causal-lock-9ad02782.interpretation: In this equation, $ds^2$ represents the squared spacetime interval, which is a measure of the "distance" between two infinitesimally separated events in spacetime. The equation $ds^2 = 0$ asserts that this interval is zero for events lying on a null geodesic. The spacetime interval is formally defined in a given spacetime geometry by the metric tensor $g_{\mu u}$ as $ds^2 = g_{\mu u} dx^\mu dx^ u$, where $dx^\mu$ and $dx^ u$ are infinitesimal coordinate displacements and the summation convention is implied. The metric tensor $g_{\mu u}$ encodes the curvature of spacetime due to mass and energy. For events separated by a null interval, they are causally connected in a way that is precisely on the boundary of what is possible for any physical signal, meaning they are connected by a signal traveling at the speed of light.
causal-lock-9ad02782.symmetry_origin: The equation $ds^2 = 0$ arises from the postulate that the speed of light in vacuum, $c$, is constant for all inertial observers, a cornerstone of Special Relativity. In General Relativity, this is extended to mean that light rays always travel along null geodesics. The invariance of the speed of light leads to the concept of spacetime intervals, and the interval for light-like paths is defined to be zero. This property is related to the conformal structure of spacetime and is fundamental to understanding causality and the propagation of information.
causal-lock-9ad02782.limits_and_boundary: The condition $ds^2 = 0$ defines the boundary between timelike intervals ( $ds^2$ 0$) and spacelike intervals ($ds^2$0$) in Minkowski spacetime (flat spacetime). Events separated by a timelike interval can be causally connected, as they are within each other's light cones. Events separated by a spacelike interval cannot be causally connected, as they lie outside each other's light cones. The equation $ds^2 = 0$ represents the paths that delineate these regions of causal influence, effectively defining the 'light cone' of an event.
causal-lock-9ad02782.conceptual_definition: The equation $ds^2 = 0$ is a fundamental concept in Einstein's theory of General Relativity, specifically describing null geodesics in spacetime. It signifies that for events connected by a null geodesic, the spacetime interval, known as the line element $ds^2$, is zero. This implies that light rays, or any massless particles traveling at the speed of light, follow paths where the temporal and spatial separations precisely cancel each other out in a relativistic sense. These paths are called null or light-like. This zero interval is a consequence of the constant speed of light, $c$, being a universal speed limit in the universe.
causal-lock-9ad02782.intuitive_summary: The path of light through spacetime has a zero interval, meaning its temporal and spatial separations are precisely balanced according to relativity.

non-conservation-identity-7d1fca43.conceptual_definition: In classical field theory, when a Lagrangian density $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{0} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{break}}$ contains a term $\mathcal{L}_{\text{break}}$ that explicitly violates an otherwise continuous symmetry parameterized by $\alpha$, the canonical Noether current $j^\mu$ associated with the transformation of $\mathcal{L}_0$ is no longer conserved on-shell. Instead, applying the Euler-Lagrange equations yields the non-conservation equation $\partial_\mu j^\mu = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{break}}}{\partial \alpha}$, relating the rate of current dissipation directly to the gradient of the explicit breaking term along the symmetry orbit.
non-conservation-identity-7d1fca43.intuitive_summary: If a physical system has an exact continuous symmetry, its Noether current is conserved ($\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$). When a perturbation explicitly spoils that symmetry, the source or sink of the current precisely matches how strongly the perturbation changes under the transformation.
non-conservation-identity-7d1fca43.description: Expresses the on-shell four-divergence of a Noether current as the variation of the symmetry-breaking Lagrangian density with respect to the transformation parameter.

mass-generation-relation-eb69497a.title: Higgs Mechanism Gauge Boson Mass Relation

M_A.name: Gauge Boson Mass
M_A.description: The rest mass of the gauge boson A.

g.name: Gauge Coupling Constant
g.description: The coupling strength of the interaction between the gauge field and the Higgs field.

v.name: Higgs Vacuum Expectation Value
v.description: The non-zero value of the Higgs field in the vacuum state, approximately 246 GeV.

mass-generation-relation-eb69497a.interpretation:
This equation quantifies the mass acquired by a gauge boson through the Higgs mechanism.
- $M_A$ is the mass of the gauge boson, for example, the $W^\pm$ or $Z^0$ bosons in the Standard Model. The mass term appears as $M_A^2$ because it originates from a term in the Lagrangian that is quadratic in the gauge fields, specifically $\frac{1}{2} M_A^2 A_\mu A^\mu$.
- $g$ is the dimensionless gauge coupling constant, which measures the strength of the interaction between the gauge boson and the Higgs field. A larger value of $g$ signifies a stronger interaction.
- $v$ is the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the Higgs field, with a value of approximately $246$ GeV. This non-zero value, acquired through spontaneous symmetry breaking, fills spacetime and is what the gauge bosons interact with to gain mass.
The formula $M_A^2 = g^2 v^2$ explicitly shows that the mass-squared is directly proportional to both the square of the coupling strength and the square of the Higgs VEV. This means particles that do not couple to the Higgs field (like the photon, for which the relevant effective coupling is zero) remain massless.
mass-generation-relation-eb69497a.symmetry_origin: Spontaneous symmetry breaking of a local gauge symmetry, such as the electroweak $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ group breaking down to the electromagnetic $U(1)_{em}$. The Higgs mechanism allows gauge bosons to acquire mass without violating the underlying gauge invariance of the Lagrangian.
mass-generation-relation-eb69497a.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of a restored symmetry where the vacuum expectation value $v \to 0$ (e.g., at very high temperatures), the gauge boson mass $M_A \to 0$. Similarly, if a boson does not couple to the Higgs field, its coupling $g \to 0$ and it remains massless, as is the case for the photon. This is a tree-level result; quantum corrections will introduce modifications to the mass via renormalization.
mass-generation-relation-eb69497a.conceptual_definition: The mass-squared $M_A^2$ of a gauge boson $A_\mu$ is generated from the kinetic term of the Higgs field Lagrangian, $|D_\mu \Phi|^2$, when the Higgs field $\Phi$ acquires a non-zero vacuum expectation value $v$. The mass is proportional to the gauge coupling constant $g$ and the VEV $v$.
mass-generation-relation-eb69497a.intuitive_summary: The Higgs field acts like a cosmic 'molasses' that permeates the universe. Gauge bosons that interact with this field experience a 'drag', which we perceive as mass. The stronger the interaction (coupling $g$) and the 'thicker' the molasses (VEV $v$), the more massive the boson becomes.
mass-generation-relation-eb69497a.description: Defines the mass of a gauge boson as generated by its interaction with the Higgs field after spontaneous electroweak symmetry breaking.

pointer-shift-b1dda340.interpretation: The initial state of the quantum system is expanded in the eigenbasis $\{|a_n\rangle\}$ of the measured observable as $|\psi\rangle = \sum_n c_n |a_n\rangle$, with complex probability amplitudes $c_n$ satisfying $\sum_n |c_n|^2 = 1$. The apparatus starts in a standardized ready state $|R_0\rangle$. The unitary interaction operator $\hat{U}_{int}$ correlates each eigenstate $|a_n\rangle$ with a macroscopically or microscopically distinct pointer state $|R_n\rangle$, where $\langle R_n | R_m \rangle = \delta_{nm}$. The resulting state $\sum_n c_n |a_n\rangle |R_n\rangle$ represents an entangled bipartite Schmidt state.
pointer-shift-b1dda340.symmetry_origin: Unitary invariance ($U(\mathcal{H}_S \otimes \mathcal{H}_R)$) under time evolution generated by the total Hermitian Hamiltonian $\hat{H} = \hat{H}_S + \hat{H}_R + \hat{H}_{int}$.
pointer-shift-b1dda340.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of zero interaction time or vanishing coupling constant ($g \to 0$), $|R_n\rangle \to |R_0\rangle$, leaving the system and apparatus completely unentangled. In the macroscopic limit (number of environmental degrees of freedom $N \to \infty$), environmental decoherence suppresses off-diagonal phase coherences between different $|R_n\rangle$ states.
pointer-shift-b1dda340.conceptual_definition: In the von Neumann measurement scheme, the pre-measurement stage involves a unitary evolution $\hat{U}_{int}$ generated by an interaction Hamiltonian between the quantum system $S$ and an apparatus or reference frame $R$. Starting from a product state $|\psi\rangle |R_0\rangle = \left(\sum_n c_n |a_n\rangle\right) |R_0\rangle$, the interaction maps each eigenstate $|a_n\rangle$ correlated to distinct orthogonal pointer states $|R_n\rangle$, establishing quantum entanglement prior to decoherence or wavefunction reduction: $|\psi\rangle |R_0\rangle \to \sum_n c_n |a_n\rangle |R_n\rangle$.
pointer-shift-b1dda340.intuitive_summary: Before a meter displays a definitive readout, its needle (pointer) becomes quantum-mechanically entangled with all possible outcomes of the system in a joint superposition.
pointer-shift-b1dda340.description: Describes the unitary interaction phase of a quantum measurement, where a system state dynamically entangles with the ready state of a measuring apparatus pointer.

time-reversal-t-identity-1-86ac6f50-b386.title: Quantum Time Reversal Operator Relation
time-reversal-t-identity-1-86ac6f50-b386.interpretation: $\hat{T}$ is the time reversal operator, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.
time-reversal-t-identity-1-86ac6f50-b386.symmetry_origin: Time-reversal invariance of the quantum state space.
time-reversal-t-identity-1-86ac6f50-b386.limits_and_boundary: Anti-linearity is required to ensure that energy eigenvalues remain positive under time reversal.

T.name: Tension / Period

time-reversal-t-identity-1-86ac6f50-b386.conceptual_definition: In quantum mechanics, the time reversal operator $\hat{T} is an anti-unitary operator. Because time reversal changes the direction of time, it must also reverse the sign of momentum and angular momentum. To preserve the canonical commutation relations$[$\hat{x}$, $\hat{p}$] = i$\hbar , the operator \hat{T} must be anti-linear, meaning it maps the imaginary unit$i$to$-i$. Consequently, \hat{T}$ acts as a complex conjugation operator in the coordinate representation.
time-reversal-t-identity-1-86ac6f50-b386.intuitive_summary: The time reversal operator in quantum mechanics is anti-unitary, which means it conjugates complex numbers, transforming the imaginary unit i into -i.

adiabatic-processes-identity-1-d37e280d-.title: Adiabatic Process Pressure-Density Relation (Polytropic Form)
adiabatic-processes-identity-1-d37e280d-.interpretation: The formula $P = K \rho^\gamma$ relates the state variables of a system undergoing a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) process. Here, $P$ represents the absolute pressure of the fluid. The term $\rho$ is the mass density of the fluid. The constant $K$ is a parameter specific to a particular adiabatic transformation, determined from initial conditions as $K = P_0 / \rho_0^\gamma$, where $P_0$ and $\rho_0$ are the initial pressure and density. The exponent $\gamma$, known as the adiabatic index or heat capacity ratio, is defined as the ratio of the specific heat at constant pressure ($C_p$) to the specific heat at constant volume ($C_v$). Its value depends on the molecular structure of the gas, e.g., $\gamma = 5/3$ for a monatomic ideal gas.
adiabatic-processes-identity-1-d37e280d-.symmetry_origin: The conservation of entropy ($dS=0$) for a reversible adiabatic process is the core principle. While not a direct Noether's theorem symmetry in the sense of spacetime symmetries, it represents an invariant quantity (entropy) under a specific class of thermodynamic transformations (reversible adiabatic changes). This invariance constrains the path taken in the state space of thermodynamic variables.
adiabatic-processes-identity-1-d37e280d-.limits_and_boundary: This relation is derived under the assumption of an ideal gas and a reversible adiabatic process. It breaks down under conditions of high density where intermolecular forces become significant, or when the process is not slow enough to be considered reversible (e.g., shock waves). For an isothermal process, where heat exchange is maximal, the relationship would be $P \propto \rho$ (Boyle's Law), which corresponds to the limit $\gamma \to 1$. The value of $\gamma$ itself depends on which molecular degrees of freedom are active, which is a function of temperature $T$.

P.description: The absolute pressure of the gas or fluid.

K.description: A constant for a specific adiabatic process, determined by the initial state and entropy of the system.

\\rho.name: Mass Density

adiabatic-processes-identity-1-d37e280d-.conceptual_definition: This equation, $P = K \rho^\gamma$, defines the relationship between the pressure $P$ and the mass density $\rho$ of a fluid (typically an ideal gas) during an adiabatic process. An adiabatic process is one that occurs without any heat transfer ($Q=0$) to or from the system. The constant $K$ is determined by the initial conditions of the system and remains constant throughout the specific adiabatic process, while $\gamma$ is the adiabatic index, a dimensionless quantity characteristic of the gas.
adiabatic-processes-identity-1-d37e280d-.intuitive_summary: Imagine squeezing a sealed, insulated container of air. As you compress it, increasing its density $\rho$, the pressure $P$ inside increases much faster than the density itself. This is because you are doing work on the gas, which increases its internal energy and temperature, leading to a sharp rise in pressure. The exponent $\gamma$, which is greater than 1, captures this non-linear, rapid pressure increase.
adiabatic-processes-identity-1-d37e280d-.description: A fundamental equation in thermodynamics and fluid dynamics that relates the pressure and mass density of a gas undergoing a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) process.

accelerated-expansion-identity-1-237e826.title: Deceleration Parameter with Cosmological Constant
accelerated-expansion-identity-1-237e826.interpretation: $q$ is the deceleration parameter. The term $\ddot{a}$ is the acceleration of the scale factor $a$, and $\dot{a}$ is its rate of expansion. The value $\Omega_m$ is the matter density parameter, and $\Omega_\Lambda$ is the dark energy density parameter.
accelerated-expansion-identity-1-237e826.symmetry_origin: Derived from the Friedmann equations under the assumption of a homogeneous, isotropic, and spatially flat universe (FLRW metric).
accelerated-expansion-identity-1-237e826.limits_and_boundary: In a matter-dominated universe ($\Omega_m = 1, \Omega_\Lambda = 0$), $q = 1/2$, indicating deceleration. In a dark energy-dominated universe ($\Omega_m = 0, \Omega_\Lambda = 1$), $q = -1$, indicating exponential de Sitter expansion. The transition from deceleration to acceleration occurs when $\Omega_\Lambda > \frac{1}{2} \Omega_m$.

completeness-quantum-identity-1-c2238e2e.title: Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) Locality Inequality
completeness-quantum-identity-1-c2238e2e.equation: |S| \le 2 \quad \text{where} \quad S = E(a, b) - E(a, b') + E(a', b) + E(a', b')
completeness-quantum-identity-1-c2238e2e.interpretation: The parameter $S$ represents the CHSH correlation parameter, constructed from the four joint expectation values $E(a, b)$, $E(a, b')$, $E(a', b)$, and $E(a', b')$. Alice selects measurement settings from $\{a, a'\}$ and Bob chooses from $\{b, b'\}$, each obtaining binary outcomes $\pm 1$. The expectation value $E(a, b) = \int A(a, \lambda) B(b, \lambda) \rho(\lambda) \, \mathrm{d}\lambda$ averages over the hidden variable distribution $\rho(\lambda)$. The local realism condition forces $|S| \le 2$.
completeness-quantum-identity-1-c2238e2e.symmetry_origin: Relativistic local causality (spacelike separation ensuring commutativity or causal independence of measurement operators) and Kolmogorovian probability theory under hidden-variable measure preservation.
completeness-quantum-identity-1-c2238e2e.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$ or for unentangled/separable quantum states ($\rho = \sum_k p_k \rho_A^k \otimes \rho_B^k$), the CHSH parameter satisfies $|S| \le 2$. In standard quantum theory, maximal entanglement allows violation up to Tsirelson's bound $|S| \le 2\sqrt{2}$. In generalized non-signaling probability theories (such as Popescu-Rohrlich PR-boxes), the algebraic maximum reaches $|S| = 4$.

Violations of this bound demonstrate quantum non-locality.
completeness-quantum-identity-1-c2238e2e.intuitive_summary: If physical properties exist independently of observation and signals cannot travel faster than light, correlated measurements between two distant parties can never exceed a score of $2$. Quantum entanglement breaks this barrier, reaching up to $2\sqrt{2}$.
completeness-quantum-identity-1-c2238e2e.description: An upper bound on statistical correlations between bipartite measurement outcomes predicted by any local hidden-variable theory.

heisenberg-uncertainty-position-momentum.title: Heisenberg uncertainty principle (position-momentum)
heisenberg-uncertainty-position-momentum.conceptual_definition: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle, in its position-momentum formulation, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics stating that there is a limit to the precision with which certain pairs of physical properties of a particle, known as complementary variables, can be known simultaneously. Specifically, it quantifies the inverse relationship between the uncertainty in a particle's position and the uncertainty in its momentum.
heisenberg-uncertainty-position-momentum.intuitive_summary: The more precisely you know where a particle is, the less precisely you can know how fast it's moving, and vice versa.
heisenberg-uncertainty-position-momentum.interpretation: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle (position-momentum) is mathematically expressed as $\Delta x \Delta k \ge 1/2$, where $\Delta x$ represents the uncertainty in the position of a particle along a given axis, and $\Delta k$ represents the uncertainty in its corresponding wave number. The wave number $k$ is directly proportional to momentum $p$ by the de Broglie relation, $p = \hbar k$, where $\hbar = h/(2\pi)$ is the reduced Planck constant. Therefore, the product of the uncertainties in position and momentum, $\Delta x \Delta p$, is related by $\Delta x \Delta p \ge \hbar/2$. This inequality signifies that it is impossible to simultaneously determine both the position and momentum of a quantum mechanical system with arbitrary precision. If $\Delta x$ is made very small (i.e., the position is known very precisely), then $\Delta k$ (and thus $\Delta p$) must be large, meaning the momentum is highly uncertain. Conversely, if the momentum is known precisely (small $\Delta p$ or $\Delta k$), then the position must be uncertain (large $\Delta x$).
heisenberg-uncertainty-position-momentum.symmetry_origin: This principle arises from the wave-particle duality inherent in quantum mechanics. Particles are described by wave functions, and the concepts of position and momentum are related through Fourier transforms. The uncertainty principle is a direct consequence of the mathematical properties of Fourier transforms, specifically that a function and its transform cannot both be sharply localized. The Fourier transform of a position-space wave function yields a momentum-space wave function, and the width of these distributions in their respective spaces are inversely related.
heisenberg-uncertainty-position-momentum.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the uncertainty in position $\Delta x$ approaches zero (a perfectly localized particle), the uncertainty in momentum $\Delta k$ approaches infinity, meaning the momentum is completely unknown. Conversely, if the uncertainty in momentum $\Delta k$ approaches zero (a particle with a perfectly defined momentum, i.e., a plane wave), the uncertainty in position $\Delta x$ approaches infinity, meaning the particle could be anywhere in space.

\\Delta x.description: The standard deviation of the probability distribution of the particle's position along a specific axis. It quantifies the range of possible positions where the particle might be found.

\\Delta k.name: Uncertainty in Wave Number
\\Delta k.description: The standard deviation of the probability distribution of the wave number of the particle's wave function. It represents the spread of possible wave numbers composing the wave packet.

\\hbar.description: A fundamental physical constant equal to Planck's constant $h$ divided by $2\pi$. It relates the energy of a photon to its frequency and is crucial in quantum mechanics, appearing in relationships like $E = \hbar \omega$ and $p = \hbar k$.

de-broglie-wavelength.title: De Broglie Wavelength
de-broglie-wavelength.conceptual_definition: The de Broglie wavelength postulate extends the wave-particle duality of light to all massive and massless matter. It defines the characteristic quantum wavelength $\lambda$ associated with a particle as the ratio of Planck's constant $h$ to the particle's canonical physical momentum $p$, expressed as $\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{2\pi \hbar}{p}$.
de-broglie-wavelength.intuitive_summary: Every moving object possesses an intrinsic wave nature; heavier and faster objects have wavelengths so tiny they appear purely classical, whereas microscopic particles exhibit observable wave interference and diffraction.
de-broglie-wavelength.interpretation: In the relation $\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$, $\lambda$ denotes the de Broglie wavelength in meters ($\text{m}$), $h$ is Planck's universal constant ($6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$), and $p$ represents the magnitude of the relativistic or non-relativistic momentum of the particle in kilograms meters per second ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}$). As momentum increases, the wavelength inversely decreases.
de-broglie-wavelength.symmetry_origin: Spatial translation invariance via Noether's theorem defines canonical momentum $\mathbf{p}$, which serves as the generator of spatial translations corresponding to wavevector $\mathbf{k}$ via $\mathbf{p} = \hbar \mathbf{k}$.
de-broglie-wavelength.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit where action $S \gg \hbar$ (or equivalently $\hbar \to 0$ / $p \to \infty$), the de Broglie wavelength vanishes ($\lambda \to 0$), recovering classical geometric ray trajectories. In the ultracold/low-momentum limit ($p \to 0$), $\lambda \to \infty$, leading to macroscopic quantum phenomena such as Bose-Einstein condensation.

\\lambda.description: Characteristic matter-wave wavelength associated with the particle

Here, $\alpha'$ is the Regge slope parameter, defining the fundamental string length scale $\ell_s = \sqrt{\alpha'}$.
tension-scale-relation.intuitive_summary: A string can wrap around a compact dimension as well as move along it; when a dimension shrinks below the string scale, winding modes become light while momentum modes become heavy, rendering the small-radius geometry physically indistinguishable from a large dual universe.
tension-scale-relation.interpretation: The variable $\tilde{R}$ denotes the dual compactification radius, $R$ represents the physical radius of the compact spatial circle, and $\alpha'$ is the universal Regge slope parameter related to the fundamental string tension $T = 1/(2\pi\alpha')$.
tension-scale-relation.symmetry_origin: Originates from the discrete $O(d,d;\mathbb{Z})$ target-space modular invariance of the 2D worldsheet conformal field theory (CFT).
tension-scale-relation.limits_and_boundary: At the self-dual point $R = \sqrt{\alpha'}$, the theory exhibits an enhanced gauge symmetry (such as $SU(2) \times SU(2)$). In the decompactification limit $R \to \infty$, $\tilde{R} \to 0$, momentum modes form a continuum and winding modes become infinitely heavy, recovering standard non-compact field theory.

einstein-field-equations-cosmological-co.title: Einstein Field Equations with Cosmological Constant
einstein-field-equations-cosmological-co.conceptual_definition: The Einstein Field Equations relate the geometry of spacetime to the distribution of matter and energy within it. This form includes the cosmological constant $\Lambda$, representing a uniform energy density of the vacuum that causes spacetime to have an intrinsic tendency to expand or contract.
einstein-field-equations-cosmological-co.intuitive_summary: Spacetime tells matter how to move, and matter tells spacetime how to curve, with the cosmological constant representing the vacuum's inherent tendency to expand.
einstein-field-equations-cosmological-co.interpretation:
The left-hand side of the equation, $G_{\mu
u} + \Lambda g_{\mu
u}$, describes the geometry of spacetime. The Einstein tensor, $G_{\mu
u}$, represents the curvature of spacetime and is defined in terms of the Ricci tensor $R_{\mu
u}$ and Ricci scalar $R$ as $G_{\mu
u} = R_{\mu
u} -  rac{1}{2} R g_{\mu
u}$. The term $\Lambda g_{\mu
u}$ introduces the cosmological constant, $\Lambda$, which acts as a source of gravity even in a vacuum, driving cosmic acceleration. The metric tensor, $g_{\mu
u}$, defines distances and angles in spacetime. The right-hand side, $ rac{8\pi G}{c^4} T_{\mu
u}$, describes the source of gravity: the distribution of matter and energy. The stress-energy tensor, $T_{\mu
u}$, is a symmetric tensor that encapsulates the density and flux of energy and momentum. The constants $G$ (Newton's gravitational constant) and $c$ (the speed of light) provide the correct proportionality between geometry and matter-energy content.
einstein-field-equations-cosmological-co.symmetry_origin:
The equations are founded on the principle of general covariance (diffeomorphism invariance), a continuous spacetime symmetry stating that the laws of physics are the same for all observers, regardless of their coordinate system. This symmetry leads to a conserved quantity via the contracted Bianchi identity, $
abla^{\mu} G_{\mu
u} = 0$, which in turn implies the local conservation of energy and momentum, $
abla^{\mu} T_{\mu
u} = 0$. The equations are derivable from the Einstein-Hilbert action with an added cosmological term.
einstein-field-equations-cosmological-co.limits_and_boundary:
1. In the weak-field limit (small curvature) and for low velocities ($v \ll c$), the equations reduce to Newton's law of universal gravitation.
2. In the absence of matter and energy ($T_{\mu\nu} = 0$) and with $\Lambda = 0$, the equations describe flat Minkowski spacetime ($G_{\mu\nu} = 0$).
3. In the absence of matter and energy ($T_{\mu\nu} = 0$) but with $\Lambda > 0$, the solution is de Sitter space, which describes an exponentially expanding universe.
4. As the cosmological constant approaches zero ($\Lambda \to 0$), the equations revert to the original Einstein Field Equations without a vacuum energy term.

proportionality-frequency-power.title: Generalized Frequency Power-Law Scaling Relation
proportionality-frequency-power.conceptual_definition: The scaling relation $\Omega \propto \omega^n$ describes physical phenomena where an observable response, power spectral density, scattering cross-section, or energy density $\Omega$ scales as the $n$-th power of the angular frequency $\omega$. Such relations arise universally in scale-invariant dynamics, linear response theory, dispersion regimes, and radiative processes (such as Rayleigh scattering where $n=4$ or thermal radiation spectra).
proportionality-frequency-power.intuitive_summary: It represents how rapidly a system's response grows, diminishes, or shifts when driven at different oscillation frequencies through a simple power-law relationship.
proportionality-frequency-power.interpretation: In this relation, $\Omega$ represents a frequency-dependent physical quantity or spectral observable. The variable $\omega$ denotes the angular frequency of the wave, field, or driver. The exponent $n$ is a real-valued scaling index or spectral index characterizing the regime of interaction. When $n > 0$, the quantity $\Omega$ grows monotonically with driving frequency; when $n < 0$, it exhibits high-frequency suppression; and $n = 0$ corresponds to a white or frequency-independent response.
proportionality-frequency-power.symmetry_origin: Scale invariance and self-similarity in the underlying differential equations or dynamical regimes, often linked to conformal or dilated symmetries in asymptotic frequency domains.
proportionality-frequency-power.limits_and_boundary: In the low-frequency limit $\omega \to 0$, the behavior is regularized by infrared cutoffs or DC response parameters. In the asymptotic ultraviolet limit $\omega \to \infty$, physical causality and Kramers-Kronig relations typically mandate $n \le 0$ to prevent divergent energy transfer, unless bounded by an ultraviolet cutoff.

sigma-approaching-infinity.title: Asymptotic Limit of a General Physical Parameter Sigma to Infinity
sigma-approaching-infinity.conceptual_definition: This expression represents a limiting case where a physical quantity, denoted by the Greek letter sigma ($\sigma$), is assumed to grow infinitely large. It is not a state that can be physically realized but serves as a powerful theoretical tool to analyze the asymptotic behavior of physical systems and simplify models. For example, in the context of electrical conductivity, the limit $\sigma \to \infty$ describes an ideal or perfect conductor.
sigma-approaching-infinity.intuitive_summary: Imagine a pipe carrying water. If the parameter $\sigma$ represents the pipe's width, the limit $\sigma \to \infty$ describes a pipe so wide it offers zero resistance to the water flow. This idealization helps us understand the maximum possible effect of that property, whether it's conductivity, interaction strength, or material stress.
sigma-approaching-infinity.interpretation: The symbol $\sigma$ is a placeholder for a scalar physical quantity whose specific meaning is context-dependent. The arrow $\to$ denotes the mathematical operation of taking a limit, and $\infty$ is the symbol for infinity, representing an unbounded increase. For instance: In electromagnetism, if $\sigma$ is the electrical conductivity, the limit $\sigma \to \infty$ describes a perfect electrical conductor (PEC), inside which the electric field $\mathbf{E}$ must be zero. In scattering theory, if $\sigma$ represents the total cross-section, the limit $\sigma \to \infty$ would imply that an incident particle is guaranteed to interact with the target, representing a 'black disk' or maximally opaque scatterer. In continuum mechanics, if $\sigma$ is the stress applied to a material, $\sigma \to \infty$ is a non-physical limit used to explore material failure points. In statistics, if $\sigma$ is the standard deviation, $\sigma \to \infty$ describes a probability distribution that is infinitely broad.
sigma-approaching-infinity.symmetry_origin: Not applicable; this is a mathematical limiting condition applied to physical variables, not a fundamental law derived from a symmetry. It is a tool used to explore the consequences of physical laws in idealized scenarios.
sigma-approaching-infinity.limits_and_boundary: This expression is itself a boundary condition used to define idealized physical models. For example, in the Drude model of conductivity, the limit $\sigma \to \infty$ corresponds to the electron scattering time $\tau \to \infty$, implying no collisions and perfect charge transport. In high-energy scattering theory, the limit $\sigma \to \infty$ often violates the unitarity bound (e.g., the Froissart bound), indicating it is a purely formal limit not achievable in a consistent quantum field theory.

kolmogorov-energy-spectrum.title: Kolmogorov -5/3 Energy Spectrum in Turbulent Flows
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum.conceptual_definition: Under Kolmogorov's 1941 hypotheses (K41) for homogeneous isotropic turbulence at high Reynolds number, the turbulent kinetic energy spectrum $E(k)$ in the inertial subrange depends solely on the mean rate of dissipation of turbulent kinetic energy per unit mass $\varepsilon$ and the wavenumber $k$, leading by dimensional analysis to the universal power-law scaling $E(k) = C \varepsilon^{2/3} k^{-5/3}$.
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum.intuitive_summary: In fully developed turbulence, kinetic energy is injected at large scales and cascades down through intermediate eddy sizes without significant viscous dissipation until reaching the smallest Kolmogorov microscale; within this intermediate inertial subrange, the distribution of energy per wavenumber follows a universal $-5/3$ power law.
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum.interpretation: In the equation $E(k) = C \varepsilon^{2/3} k^{-5/3}$, $E(k)$ represents the one-dimensional energy spectrum function with units of $\text{m}^3\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$, such that the total turbulent kinetic energy per unit mass is $\int_0^\infty E(k)\,dk$. The parameter $\varepsilon$ is the average rate of turbulent energy dissipation per unit mass with dimensions $\text{m}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-3}$. The variable $k$ is the spatial wavenumber ($k = 2\pi / \lambda$), inversely related to eddy size $\lambda$. The prefactor $C$ is the dimensionless universal Kolmogorov constant, typically found empirically to be $C \approx 1.4 - 1.7$.
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum.symmetry_origin: Statistical scale invariance and rotational/translational symmetry (statistical homogeneity and isotropy) of the Navier-Stokes equations in the high Reynolds number limit away from boundaries.
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $k \to 0$ (integral scale / energy injection range $k \sim L^{-1}$), the spectrum deviates from $k^{-5/3}$ and is governed by geometry-dependent energy injection ($E(k) \propto k^2$ or $k^4$). In the limit $k \to \infty$ beyond the Kolmogorov dissipation wavenumber $\\beta^{-1} = (\varepsilon / \nu^3)^{1/4}$, viscous dissipation dominates and $E(k)$ decays exponentially.

planck-length-definition-626db741.title: Definition of the Planck Length
planck-length-definition-626db741.description: The Planck length is the fundamental unit of length in the Planck natural unit system, representing the characteristic spatial scale at which quantum gravitational effects dominate.
planck-length-definition-626db741.conceptual_definition: The Planck length $\ell_P$ is uniquely constructed via dimensional analysis from three fundamental physical constants: the reduced Planck constant $\hbar$, the Newtonian gravitational constant $G$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c$. It defines the spatial scale at which the reduced Compton wavelength $\b\bar{\lambda}} = \hbar / (M c)$ of a mass $M$ becomes equal to half its Schwarzschild radius $r_s / 2 = G M / c^2$, marking the transition where quantum mechanics and general relativity simultaneously govern spacetime dynamics.
planck-length-definition-626db741.interpretation: In this formula, $\ell_P$ denotes the Planck length ($[\text{L}]$), $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant governing quantum action ($[\text{M}][\text{L}]^2[\text{T}]^{-1}$), $G$ is the universal gravitational constant parameterizing spacetime curvature ($[\text{M}]^{-1}[\text{L}]^3[\text{T}]^{-2}$), and $c$ is the invariant speed of light relating space and time ($[\text{L}][\text{T}]^{-1}$). Combining these parameters yields a unique length scale of order $\approx 1.616 \times 10^{-35} \text{ m}$. Below this scale, localizing a particle within its Compton wavelength requires an energy density that collapses the localized region into a microscopic black hole.
planck-length-definition-626db741.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, $\ell_P \to 0$, restoring a smooth, continuous spacetime continuum. In the non-gravitational limit $G \to 0$, $\ell_P \to 0$, reducing physics to standard relativistic quantum field theory in flat Minkowski space. In the non-relativistic limit $c \to \infty$, $\ell_P \to 0$, decoupling spacetime structure from quantum action.
planck-length-definition-626db741.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the unification of global spacetime symmetries: the Lorentz invariance of special relativity ($c$), the general covariance (diffeomorphism invariance) of general relativity ($G$), and the unitary phase transformations of quantum mechanics ($\hbar$).

principal-quantum-number-for-third-energ.title: Principal Quantum Number for the Third Energy Level
principal-quantum-number-for-third-energ.description: Specifies the discrete principal quantum number $n = 3$, identifying the third principal electron shell (M-shell) in hydrogenic and multi-electron atomic systems.
principal-quantum-number-for-third-energ.conceptual_definition: The principal quantum number $n$ labels the discrete bound eigenstates of the central-potential Coulomb Hamiltonian. Setting $n = 3$ designates the third principal shell ($M$-shell), corresponding to degenerate subshells with orbital angular momentum quantum numbers $l \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ ($3s$, $3p$, and $3d$ orbitals) and a total spatial orbital degeneracy of $n^2 = 9$ (or $2n^2 = 18$ including electron spin).
principal-quantum-number-for-third-energ.interpretation: The parameter $n$ is the principal quantum number. In a non-relativistic hydrogenic atom of nuclear charge $Z$, setting $n = 3$ fixes the quantized energy level to $E_3 = -\frac{Z^2 e^4 m_e}{32 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 \hbar^2 \cdot 3^2} = -\frac{13.6\text{ eV} \cdot Z^2}{9}$, and sets the mean orbital radius $\langle r \rangle_{3,l} \sim \frac{a_0}{Z} \left[\frac{3}{2} n^2 - \frac{1}{2} l(l+1)\right]$.
principal-quantum-number-for-third-energ.limits_and_boundary: In the classical correspondence limit ($n \to \infty$), the energy spacing $\Delta E = E_{n+1} - E_n \to 0$, recovering the continuous classical orbital frequency according to Bohr's correspondence principle. At $n = 1$, the system minimizes energy into the ground state.
principal-quantum-number-for-third-energ.symmetry_origin: Arises from the spherical symmetry $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and the dynamical Runge-Lenz symmetry $\mathrm{SO}(4)$ of the $1/r$ Coulomb potential, which enforces energy degeneracy across all angular momentum channels $l < n$.

principal-quantum-number-for-third-energ.intuitive_summary: In atomic physics, $n=3$ denotes the third orbital tier from the nucleus, establishing the radial scale and bound energy of the electron state, famously serving as the upper level for the $H_\alpha$ Balmer emission line ($n=3 \to 2$) and the lower level for the Paschen series ($n \to 3$).

moment-of-inertia-of-a-system-component-.title: Principal Moment of Inertia (First Axis)
moment-of-inertia-of-a-system-component-.description: Quantifies the rotational inertia of a rigid body or multi-component system about its first principal axis of rotation, relating angular velocity along that axis to the corresponding component of angular momentum.
moment-of-inertia-of-a-system-component-.conceptual_definition: The principal moment of inertia $I_1$ is the eigenvalue of the moment of inertia tensor corresponding to the first principal axis of rotation. In a coordinate frame aligned with the body's principal axes, the moment of inertia tensor becomes diagonal, simplifying the relation between angular momentum and angular velocity to $L_1 = I_1 \omega_1$. It represents the resistance of the mass distribution to angular acceleration about the primary axis.
moment-of-inertia-of-a-system-component-.interpretation: The symbol $I_1$ represents the principal scalar moment of inertia along the body-fixed principal axis $\mathbf{e}_1$. For a discrete or continuous mass distribution, $I_1 = \int \rho(\mathbf{r})(x_2^2 + x_3^2)\,d^3\mathbf{r}$. It directly governs the rotational kinetic energy contribution $T_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2$ and enters Euler's dynamical equations for rigid body rotation.
moment-of-inertia-of-a-system-component-.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where all mass collapses to the rotation axis ($r_\perp \to 0$), $I_1 \to 0$. In the continuum limit of an extended body of mass $M$ and characteristic dimension $R$, $I_1 \propto M R^2$. Under uniform spherical symmetry, $I_1 = I_2 = I_3$.
moment-of-inertia-of-a-system-component-.symmetry_origin: Rotational invariance in isotropic space leads to conservation of total angular momentum via Noether's theorem; diagonalizing the symmetric rank-2 inertia tensor identifies the principal axes reflecting the geometric symmetry of the mass distribution.

non-relativistic-degenerate-electron-gas.title: Non-Relativistic Degenerate Electron Gas Pressure Scaling
non-relativistic-degenerate-electron-gas.description: Describes the polytropic equation of state scaling for a completely degenerate, non-relativistic electron gas where quantum degeneracy pressure scales with mass density as $\rho^{5/3}$.
non-relativistic-degenerate-electron-gas.conceptual_definition: For a zero-temperature Fermi gas of non-relativistic electrons, the Pauli exclusion principle forces electrons into high-momentum quantum states up to the Fermi momentum $p_F = \hbar (3\pi^2 n_e)^{1/3}$. Because the electron kinetic energy scales quadratically with momentum ($E_k = p^2 / 2m_e$), the volumetric energy density scales as $u \propto n_e^{5/3}$, yielding a degeneracy pressure $P = \frac{2}{3}u \propto \rho^{5/3}$ when number density $n_e$ is proportional to mass density $\rho$.
non-relativistic-degenerate-electron-gas.interpretation: In this scaling relation, $P$ represents the isotropic degeneracy pressure exerted by electrons and $\rho$ denotes the total mass density of the stellar or laboratory plasma. The exponent $5/3$ corresponds to an adiabatic polytrope of index $n = 3/2$ (or adiabatic index $\Gamma = 5/3$). This relation dictates the mechanical structure of low-mass white dwarfs, where electron degeneracy pressure stabilizes the stellar core against gravitational collapse without requiring thermal energy support.
non-relativistic-degenerate-electron-gas.limits_and_boundary: As density increases such that the Fermi momentum approaches the relativistic regime ($p_F \sim m_e c$), the kinetic energy-momentum relation transitions from $E \propto p^2$ to $E \propto p c$, shifting the pressure scaling asymptotically from $P \propto \rho^{5/3}$ to the ultra-relativistic limit $P \propto \rho^{4/3}$. In the classical thermal limit where thermal energy dominates over Fermi energy ($k_B T \gg E_F$), the equation transitions back to the ideal gas law $P \propto \rho T$. In the formal classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the degeneracy pressure vanishes.
non-relativistic-degenerate-electron-gas.symmetry_origin: Permutation antisymmetry of the multiparticle fermionic wavefunction under spatial and spin exchange (Pauli exclusion principle), coupled with spatial translational and rotational invariance of isotropic momentum phase space.

In the non-relativistic regime, faster speeds mean both more frequent collisions and higher momentum transfer, compounding into a pressure that grows faster than density to the $5/3$ power.

rest-mass-energy-squared-term-2f9f4d40.title: Invariant Mass-Momentum Squared Term
rest-mass-energy-squared-term-2f9f4d40.description: Represents the Lorentz-invariant scalar term $m_0^2 c^2$ appearing in the relativistic dispersion relation $(E/c)^2 - p^2 = m_0^2 c^2$, quantifying the invariant norm of a particle's four-momentum.
rest-mass-energy-squared-term-2f9f4d40.conceptual_definition: The quantity $m_0^2 c^2$ is the product of the squared invariant rest mass $m_0^2$ and the square of the speed of light $c^2$. It defines the invariant magnitude squared of a relativistic particle's four-momentum in momentum units $(p^\mu p_\mu = m_0^2 c^2)$ under the Minkowski metric signature $(+,-,-,-)$, acting as the fundamental Casimir invariant of the Poincaré group.
rest-mass-energy-squared-term-2f9f4d40.interpretation: The term $m_0^2 c^2$ is constructed from the rest mass $m_0$ and the universal speed of light $c$. In momentum space, it serves as the square of the characteristic momentum scale $p_0 = m_0 c$. When multiplied by $c^2$, it yields the squared rest energy $E_0^2 = m_0^2 c^4$. In the relativistic energy-momentum invariant $(E/c)^2 - p^2 = m_0^2 c^2$, it fixes the mass shell condition separating timelike ($m_0^2 > 0$), lightlike ($m_0 = 0$), and spacelike ($m_0^2 < 0$) trajectories.
rest-mass-energy-squared-term-2f9f4d40.limits_and_boundary: In the massless limit $m_0 \to 0$, the invariant term vanishes ($m_0^2 c^2 \to 0$), yielding the dispersion relation for photons and other ultra-relativistic particles $E = pc$. In the non-relativistic limit $v \ll c$, total momentum $p \ll m_0 c$, reducing the full relation to $E \approx m_0 c^2 + p^2/(2m_0)$.
rest-mass-energy-squared-term-2f9f4d40.symmetry_origin: Originates from Poincaré spacetime symmetry (Lorentz invariance and spacetime translation invariance), corresponding to the first Casimir invariant $P^\mu P_\mu = m_0^2 c^2$ which classifies irreducible unitary representations of the Poincaré group.

non-commuting-operators-condition-37c704.title: Non-Commuting Operators Condition in Quantum Mechanics
non-commuting-operators-condition-37c704.description: Specifies that the Lie bracket (commutator) of two quantum mechanical operators is non-zero, establishing that the associated physical observables are incompatible and cannot share a complete set of simultaneous eigenstates.
non-commuting-operators-condition-37c704.conceptual_definition: In quantum mechanics, two linear operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ acting on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ are said to be non-commuting if their commutator bracket does not vanish: $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \equiv \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A} \neq 0$. This algebraic property serves as the foundational mathematical condition for incompatible observables, enforcing the generalized Robertson-Schrödinger uncertainty relation $\sigma_A \sigma_B \ge \frac{1}{2}|\langle [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \rangle|$ and precluding the existence of a common eigenbasis.
non-commuting-operators-condition-37c704.interpretation: The condition $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \neq 0$ asserts that the successive application of the operator $\hat{A}$ and the operator $\hat{B}$ onto an arbitrary state vector $|\psi\rangle \in \mathcal{H}$ is non-Abelian ($\hat{A}\hat{B}|\psi\rangle \neq \hat{B}\hat{A}|\psi\rangle$). Consequently, the physical observables corresponding to self-adjoint operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ cannot be measured simultaneously to arbitrary precision, and preparing a state in a definite eigenstate of $\hat{A}$ necessarily induces dispersion in the measurement outcomes of $\hat{B}$.
non-commuting-operators-condition-37c704.limits_and_boundary: In the classical correspondence limit where Planck's constant $\hbar \to 0$, the quantum commutator divided by $i\hbar$ transitions via Dirac canonical quantization to the classical Poisson bracket, $\frac{1}{i\hbar}[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \to \{A, B\}_{\text{PB}}$, where classical observables commute under ordinary multiplication.
non-commuting-operators-condition-37c704.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the non-commutative Lie algebra of the symmetry group generating quantum transformations (such as the Heisenberg-Weyl algebra $[\hat{x}_j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar \delta_{jk}\hat{I}$ arising from spatial translations and the rotation group $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ algebra $[\hat{J}_i, \hat{J}_j] = i\hbar \epsilon_{ijk}\hat{J}_k$).

grand-unification-energy-scale-value-32c.title: Grand Unification Energy Scale Magnitude
grand-unification-energy-scale-value-32c.description: Numerical value of the energy scale ($\approx 2 \times 10^{16}\text{ GeV}$) at which the gauge coupling constants of the $SU(3)_C$, $SU(2)_L$, and $U(1)_Y$ interactions unify within minimal supersymmetric grand unified theories.
grand-unification-energy-scale-value-32c.conceptual_definition: The energy value $2 \times 10^{16}\text{ GeV}$ denotes the characteristic grand unification energy scale ($M_{\text{GUT}}$). Extrapolated using the Renormalization Group Equations (RGEs) of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), the three gauge couplings converge at this energy scale, below which the unified simple gauge group (such as $SU(5)$ or $SO(10)$) spontaneously breaks down to the Standard Model gauge group $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$.
grand-unification-energy-scale-value-32c.interpretation: The energy scale $M_{\text{GUT}} \approx 2 \times 10^{16}\text{ GeV}$ sets the mass scale for heavy leptoquark gauge bosons $X$ and $Y$ ($M_X \sim M_{\text{GUT}}$), mediating proton decay. The scale is situated roughly three orders of magnitude below the reduced Planck mass ($M_{\text{Pl}} \approx 2.4 \times 10^{18}\text{ GeV}$), protecting gauge coupling unification from dominant quantum gravitational corrections.
grand-unification-energy-scale-value-32c.limits_and_boundary: At energies $\mu \ll 2 \times 10^{16}\text{ GeV}$, effective field theory applies and running couplings diverge according to Standard Model RGE beta functions. At $\mu \sim 2 \times 10^{16}\text{ GeV}$, full unified gauge symmetry is restored. At $\mu \to M_{\text{Pl}} \sim 10^{19}\text{ GeV}$, quantum gravity effects become non-perturbative.
grand-unification-energy-scale-value-32c.symmetry_origin: Spontaneous symmetry breaking of a simple grand unified gauge group (e.g., $SO(10)$, $SU(5)$, or $E_6$) down to the Standard Model subgroup $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ driven by the vacuum expectation value of an adjoint or higher-dimensional scalar representation.
